text: Let [TeX: \mathcal{G}=\{G_{1},\dots,G_{N}\}] denotes [TeX: N] graphs. For each graph [TeX: G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X})] , [TeX: \mathcal{V}] is the set of nodes, [TeX: \mathcal{E}] is the set of edges and [TeX: \mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\},\mathbf{x}_{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}] is the [TeX: d] -dimensional node feature for each node in [TeX: \mathcal{V}] . We denote [TeX: \mathcal{Y}=\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{M}\}] as [TeX: M] labels and a label set Y is a set of labels selected from [TeX: \mathcal{Y}] . The G-Meta’s core principle is to represent nodes with local subgraphs and then use subgraphs to easily transfer knowledge across tasks, graphs, and label sets. We use [TeX: \mathcal{S}] to denote local subgraphs for nodes, [TeX: \mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{n}\}] . Hence, the classification task is to learn a GNN [TeX: f_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\mapsto\{1,\dots,|\textsc{Y}|\}] , i.e., to correctly map node [TeX: u] ’s local subgraph [TeX: S_{u}] to labels in Y given only a handful of labeled nodes.

Background on Graph Neural Networks. GNNs learn compact representations, i.e., embeddings, that capture network structure and node features. The input to GNN is a graph [TeX: G] . The output is generated via a series of propagation layers [10]. Propagation at layer [TeX: l] consists of three steps: (1) Message passing. GNN computes a message [TeX: \mathbf{m}^{(l)}_{uv}=\textsc{Msg}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(l-1)},\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(l-1)})] for every linked nodes [TeX: u,v] based on their embeddings from the previous layer [TeX: \mathbf{h}_{u}^{(l-1)}] and [TeX: \mathbf{h}_{v}^{(l-1)}] . (2) Neighborhood aggregation. The messages between node [TeX: u] and its neighbors [TeX: \mathcal{N}_{u}] are aggregated as [TeX: \hat{\mathbf{m}}^{(l)}_{u}=\textsc{Agg}({\mathbf{m}^{(l)}_{uv}|v\in\mathcal{N}_{u}})] . (3) Update. Finally, GNN uses a non-linear function to update embeddings [TeX: \mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{u}=\textsc{Upd}(\hat{\mathbf{m}}^{(l)}_{u},\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_{u})] using the aggregated message and the embedding from the previous layer, for each node [TeX: u] .

Background on Meta-learning. In meta-learning, we have a meta-set [TeX: \mathscr{D}] that consists of [TeX: \mathscr{D}_{\text{train}},\mathscr{D}_{\text{val}},\mathscr{D}_{\text{test}}] . This meta-set consists of many tasks. Each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}\in\mathscr{D}] can be divided into [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{support}}] and [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{query}}] . [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{support}}] has [TeX: \textsc{k}_{\text{support}}] labeled data points in each label for learning and [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{query}}] has [TeX: \textsc{k}_{\text{query}}] data points in each label for evaluation. The size of the label set for the meta-set [TeX: |\textsc{Y}|] is N. It is also called N-ways [TeX: \textsc{k}_{\text{support}}] -shots learning problem. During meta-training, for [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}] from [TeX: \mathscr{D}_{\text{train}}] , the model first learns from [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{support}}] and then evaluates on [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{query}}] to see how well the model performs on that task. The goal of Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) [9] is to obtain a parameter initialization [TeX: \theta_{*}] that can adapt to unseen tasks quickly, such as [TeX: \mathscr{D}_{\text{test}}] , using gradients information learnt during meta-training. Hyperparameters are tuned via [TeX: \mathscr{D}_{\text{val}}] .

G-Meta is an approach that can tackle three fundamentally different meta-learning problems (Figure 1). Shared label refers that every task shares the same label set Y. Disjoint label refers to the situation where the label sets for tasks [TeX: i] and [TeX: j] are disjoint, i.e., [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}\cap\textsc{Y}_{j}=\emptyset] . Each data point in a task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}] is a local subgraph [TeX: S_{u}] , along with its associated label [TeX: Y_{u}] . The overall goal is to adapt to an unseen task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{*}\sim p(\mathcal{T})] with a few examples after observing related tasks [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}\sim p(\mathcal{T})] .

Graph meta-learning problem 1: Single Graph and Disjoint Labels. We have a graph [TeX: G] with a distribution of label set [TeX: p(\textsc{Y}|G)] . The goal is to adapt to an unseen label set [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{*}\sim p(\textsc{Y}|G)] by learning from tasks with other label sets [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}\sim p(\textsc{Y}|G)] , where [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}\cap\textsc{Y}_{*}=\emptyset] for every label set [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}] .

Graph meta-learning problem 2: Multiple Graphs and Shared Labels. We have a distribution of graphs [TeX: p(G)] but one label set Y. The goal is to learn from another graph [TeX: G_{j}\sim p(G)] and quickly adapt to an unseen graph [TeX: G_{*}\sim p(G)] , where [TeX: G_{j}] and [TeX: G_{*}] are disjoint. All tasks share the same labels.

Graph meta-learning problem 3: Multiple Graphs and Disjoint Labels. We have a distribution of label sets [TeX: p(\textsc{Y}|\mathcal{G})] conditioned on multiple graphs [TeX: \mathcal{G}] . In contrast to Problem 1, each task has its own label set [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}] but those label sets can appear in one or more graphs. The goal is to adapt to an unseen label set [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{*}\sim p(\textsc{Y}|\mathcal{G})] after learning from some other label set [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}\sim p(\textsc{Y}|\mathcal{G})] , where [TeX: \textsc{Y}_{i}\cap\textsc{Y}_{*}=\emptyset] .
5 G-Meta: Meta Learning via Local Subgraphs

Figure 2: (1) We first construct a batch of [TeX: m] meta-training tasks and extract local subgraphs on the fly for nodes in the meta-tasks. For each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}] , (2) subgraphs from the support set are mini-batched and are fed into a GNN parameterized by [TeX: \theta] . (3) The support set embeddings using the centroid nodes are generated, and (4) the prototypes are computed from the support centroid embeddings. Then, (5) the support set loss [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{support}}] is computed, and (6) back-propagates to update the GNN parameter. (7) [TeX: \mathcal{T}^{\text{query}}_{i}] subgraphs then feed into the updated GNN to (8) generate query centroid embeddings. (9) Using the support prototypes and the query embeddings, the query loss [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{query}}^{i}] for task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}] is computed. Steps (2-9) are repeated for [TeX: \eta] update steps. The same process repeats for the other [TeX: m] sampled tasks, starting from the same GNN [TeX: f_{\theta}] . (10) The last update step’s query loss from all the tasks are summed up and used to update [TeX: \theta] . Then, another batch of tasks are sampled, and step (1-10) are repeated. Then, for meta-testing tasks, steps (1-9) are repeated with the GNN using the meta-learned parameter [TeX: \theta_{*}] , which enables generalization over unseen tasks. See Algorithm 1 (Appendix E).

G-Meta (Figure 2) is an approach for meta-learning on graphs. Building on theoretical motivation from Section 4, G-Meta first constructs local subgraphs. It then uses a GNN encoder to generate centroid embeddings for subgraphs. Finally, it uses prototypical loss for inductive bias and MAML for knowledge transfer across graphs and labels. The overview is in Algorithm 1 (Appendix E).

Neural encoding of subgraph centroids. In each meta-task, we first construct subgraphs for each node. Then, each subgraph [TeX: S_{u}] is fed into a [TeX: h] -layer GNN to obtain an embedding for every node in the subgraph. [TeX: h] is set to be the subgraph neighborhood size. The centroid node [TeX: u] ’s embedding is used to represent the subgraph [TeX: \mathbf{h}_{u}=\text{GNN}(S_{u})_{\mathrm{centroid}}] . We use centroid node embedding instead of a readout function such as sum/mean over every node in the subgraph, as in the typical graph classification settings [44, 4]. The reason is that as we relax [TeX: h] to be a large number, the subgraph could potentially be large. A standard readout function over every node in the subgraph may add noise. When [TeX: h] is set to be the graph’s diameter, the centroid embedding is the same as the node embedding generated by applying GNN on the entire graph. Note that for faster computation, we mini-batch the subgraphs for each meta-task’s support and query set.

Prototypical loss. After we obtain a sufficient subgraph representation, we further leverage the inductive bias between representation and labels to circumvent the problem of scarce label information for effective propagation in the few-shot settings. For each label [TeX: k] , we take the mean of the support set subgraph embeddings to obtain prototype [TeX: \mathbf{c}_{k}] : [TeX: \mathbf{c}_{k}=1/N_{k}\sum_{y_{j}=k}\mathbf{h}_{j}] . The prototype [TeX: \mathbf{c}_{k}] serves as a landmark for the label [TeX: k] . Then, for each local subgraph [TeX: S_{u}] in both support and query set, a class distribution vector [TeX: \mathbf{p}] is computed via the euclidean distance between the support prototypes for each class and the subgraph centroid embeddings: [TeX: \mathbf{p}_{k}=\frac{\mathrm{exp}\left(-\|\mathbf{h}_{u}-\mathbf{c}_{k}\|\right)}{\sum_{\hat{k}}\mathrm{exp}\left(-\|\mathbf{h}_{u}-\mathbf{c}_{\hat{k}}\|\right)}] . After obtaining a prediction probability distribution over label classes [TeX: \mathbf{p}] for each local subgraph [TeX: S_{u}] , a cross-entropy loss is used to backpropagate [TeX: \mathrm{L}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j}\;\mathrm{log}\;\mathbf{p}_{j}] , where [TeX: \mathbf{y}] is the true label’s one hot encoding.

Optimization-based meta-learning. To transfer the structural knowledge across graphs and labels, we use MAML, an optimization-based meta-learning approach. We break the node’s dependency on a graph by framing nodes into independent local subgraph classification tasks. It allows direct adaptation to MAML since individual subgraphs can be considered as an individual image in the classic few-shot meta-learning setups. More specifically, we first sample a batch of tasks, where each task consists of a set of subgraphs. During meta-training inner loop, we perform the regular stochastic gradient descent on the support loss for each task [TeX: \mathcal{T}_{i}] : [TeX: \theta_{j}=\theta_{j-1}-\alpha\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{support}}] . The updated parameter is then evaluated using the query set, and the query loss for task [TeX: i] is recorded as [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{query}}^{i}] . The above steps are repeated for [TeX: \eta] update steps. Then, the [TeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{query}}^{i}] from the last update step is summed up across the batch of tasks, and then we perform a meta-update step: [TeX: \theta=\theta-\beta\nabla\sum_{i}\mathcal{L}_{\text{query}}^{i}] . Next, new tasks batch are sampled, and the same iteration is applied on the meta-updated [TeX: \theta] . During meta-testing, the same procedure above is applied using the final meta-updated parameter [TeX: \theta_{*}] . [TeX: \theta_{*}] is learned from knowledge across meta-training tasks and is the optimal parameter to adapt to unseen tasks quickly.

Attractive properties of G-Meta. (1) Scalability: G-Meta operates on a mini-batch of local subgraphs where the subgraph size and the batch size (few-shots) are both small. This allows fast computation and low memory requirement because G-Meta’s aggregation field is smaller than that of previous methods that operate on entire graphs [2, 50]. We further increase scalability by sub-sampling subgraphs with more than 1,000 nodes. (2) Inductive learning: Since G-Meta operates on different subgraphs in each GNN encoding, it forces inductiveness over unseen subgraphs. This inductiveness is crucial for few-shot learning, where the trained model needs to adapt to unseen nodes. Inductive learning also allows for knowledge transfer from meta-training subgraphs to meta-testing subgraphs. (3) Few-shot learning: G-Meta needs only a tiny number of labeled nodes for successful learning, as demonstrated in experiments. This property is in contrast with prevailing GNNs, which require a large fraction of labeled nodes to propagate neural messages in the graph successfully. (4) Broad applicability: G-Meta applies to many graph meta-learning problems (Figure 1) whereas previous methods apply to at most one [2, 50]. Unlike earlier methods, G-Meta works for node classification and also few-shot link prediction (i.e., via local subgraphs for a pair of nodes).

Experimental setup. (1) Node classification. For disjoint label setups, we sample 5 labels for meta-testing, 5 for meta-validation, and use the rest for meta-training. For multiple graph setups, 10% (10%) of all graphs are held out for testing (validation). The remaining graphs are used for training. In each task, 2-ways 1-shot learning is used for synthetic datasets and 3-ways 3-shots learning for real-world datasets. (2) Link prediction. 10% of graphs are held out for testing and another 10% for validation. For each graph, the support set consists of 30% edges and the query set 70%. Negative edges are sampled randomly to match the same number of positive edges, and we follow the experiment setting from [49] to construct the training graph. We use 16-shots for each task, i.e., using only 32 node pairs to predict links for an unseen graph. Hyperparameters are in Appendix G.

Appendix I Further Details on Performance Evaluation
All of our experiments are done on an Intel Xeon CPU 2.50GHz and using an NVIDIA K80 GPU.

For synthetic datasets disjoint label problems, we use a 2-way setup. In the shared label problem, the cycle graph has 17 labels and the BA graph has 10 labels. The results use 5 gradient update steps in meta-training and 10 gradient update steps in meta-testing. For real-world datasets node classification uses 3-shots and link prediction uses 16-shots. For disjoint labels problems, we set it to 3-way classification task. The results use 10 gradient update steps in meta-training and 10 gradient update steps in meta-testing. For Tissue-PPI, we have ten 2-way protein function tasks average where each task is performed three times.

For link prediction problem, to ensure the support and query set are distinct in all meta-training tasks, we separate a fixed 30% of edges for support set and 70% of edges for query set as a preprocessing step for every graph.
